title: Analysis: China’s quarterly CO2 falls 3% in largest drop since Covid - Carbon Brief
gist: China's CO2 emissions fell 3.1% year-on-year in Q3 2026, the biggest quarterly drop since the 2022 Covid lockdowns, as coal-power generation fell 3.3%, transport oil use dropped 9% amid the Hormuz crisis and EV adoption (67% of car sales, 50% of heavy trucks), and coal-to-chemicals growth slowed. Clean power additions outpaced demand growth more than twofold, extending a flat-or-falling emissions trend since March 2024, while ongoing coal-plant construction is eroding coal plant utilisation and profits.

insights.claim: China's CO2 emissions fell 3.1% year-on-year in Q3 2026, the largest quarterly reduction since the 2022 Covid lockdowns, bringing year-to-date emissions down an estimated 0.5%.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case that China's emissions have peaked, a key input for global fossil-fuel demand forecasts.

insights.claim: In Q3 2026 China's coal use fell 3% year-on-year and oil use fell 4%.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Simultaneous declines in China's coal and oil demand are bearish for seaborne coal and crude exporters.
insights.locator: The new analysis for Carbon Brief

insights.claim: China's CO2 emissions have been in a flat-or-falling trend since March 2024, now lasting more than two years.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A sustained multi-year plateau suggests a structural rather than cyclical shift in Chinese fossil demand.

insights.claim: China's coal-power generation fell 3.3% in Q3 2026 as electricity demand growth slowed and curtailment of wind and solar power declined.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Lower curtailment means each new renewable gigawatt displaces more coal, accelerating thermal coal demand decline.
insights.locator: Key drivers of the fall in CO2

insights.claim: China's solar, wind and nuclear generation rose 110 TWh year-on-year in Q3 2026, more than twice the growth in total electricity demand and equal to Germany's total power output in the same period.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Clean supply growth outrunning demand is the mechanism forcing fossil generation down in China.
insights.quote: This added clean-power generation equal to Germany’s total power output in the same time period.
insights.locator: Power generation from solar, wind and nuclear

insights.claim: China continues to build new coal-power capacity at near-record rates even as coal generation falls, so average coal plant running hours are falling faster than total generation and eroding coal plant profits.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Chinese coal generators face a stranded-asset and margin squeeze, pressuring utility earnings and possibly prompting capacity payment reforms.

insights.claim: Clean-power generation growth in China is likely to exceed total energy demand growth in 2026, maintaining a structural fall in fossil-fuel use.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Points to a full-year 2026 decline in Chinese fossil fuel consumption.

insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Grid, transmission and storage investment in China is the bottleneck to watch.

themes.theme: EVs and Hormuz crush oil demand

insights.claim: China's transport oil consumption fell 9% year-on-year in Q3 2026, with the Hormuz crisis continuing to hit oil demand.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A supply shock is accelerating demand destruction in the world's largest crude importer, which may not reverse when supply normalises.

insights.claim: Electric vehicles reached a record 67% of China's passenger car sales and 50% of heavy truck sales in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Electrification of heavy trucks at 50% share threatens diesel demand, previously seen as harder to displace.
insights.quote: hitting a record 67% of passenger car sales and 50% of heavy trucks in September

insights.claim: Electricity used by EVs in China grew 53%, much faster than the EV fleet, indicating drivers are using existing EVs in preference to fuelled vehicles.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Usage shift within mixed-fleet households amplifies oil displacement beyond what EV sales numbers alone suggest.

insights.claim: Growth in China's coal-to-chemical industry, a key source of emissions growth, continued to slow in Q3 2026 because high coal prices weakened profitability and higher output prices hurt downstream demand.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Removes one of the last growth legs for Chinese coal demand.

insights.claim: CO2 emissions from China's cement and steel production continued to fall in Q3 2026 as the contraction in construction volumes accelerated.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Accelerating construction contraction is bearish for iron ore and coking coal demand.

insights.claim: The outlook for China's CO2 emissions depends on the balance between rising energy demand, clean-energy growth and the government's response to a GDP slowdown.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Stimulus decisions are the swing factor for whether China's emissions decline persists.

insights.claim: China's recent slowdown in energy demand growth is only partly explained by exceptionally mild Q3 2026 weather, with weaker GDP growth another key factor.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Part of the decline is weather-driven and could reverse in a hotter or colder quarter.

insights.claim: Because China's reported GDP growth remains within target, there is reduced pressure for further stimulus, and the stimulus announced so far focuses on 'six networks' including the power grid and transport, which are covered by green and zero-carbon policies.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Chinese stimulus is unlikely to trigger a heavy-industry emissions rebound and favours grid and transport infrastructure plays.

insights.claim: Chinese energy consumption growth has been falling after a period of exceptionally high growth during Covid, while clean-power growth has remained robust.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Normalising demand growth makes it easier for clean supply to cover all incremental demand.
